name: Volufiline

lead: Volufiline is a cosmetic ingredient from Sederma, a Croda company. It is a blend of hydrogenated polyisobutene and an extract of Anemarrhena asphodeloides root whose compound sarsasapogenin is said to push pre-fat cells to mature and store lipid. It is sold alone or in serums aimed at hollow under-eyes, smile lines, lips, breasts and buttocks.

The company's published trial used a 5 percent cream on one breast in 28 women for 56 days, with an average volume rise of 2.2 percent against 0.9 percent in controls and up to 8.4 percent in best responders. Facial results come from user reports, including before-and-after posts on looksmax.org.

paras: Users apply a small amount of the oil-like product to the target area, commonly at night, and often for weeks to months, sometimes mixed with a moisturizer. Forum posters report lip and under-eye changes after two to three months, while other members say they saw nothing.

Reported effects are mild irritation, redness, itching and allergic reactions, and patch testing is generally advised. Long-term safety is not well documented and volume is said to reverse after stopping. It is regulated as a cosmetic ingredient, not a drug.

chain: Topical extract applied over a hollow or thin area
Sarsasapogenin is said to stimulate local fat-cell growth and lipid storage
angle.text: Users apply Volufiline to under-eyes, lips or smile lines hoping to rebuild small amounts of local volume without injectable filler. Reports describe changes appearing over weeks to months.

lead: Volufiline is a proprietary cosmetic ingredient made by the French firm Sederma, a member of Croda International. Its INCI name is hydrogenated polyisobutene plus Anemarrhena asphodeloides root extract: an oil-soluble carrier holding a plant-derived sarsasapogenin, which the maker describes as a phytosterol with no hormonal activity.[1][2]

People use it to try to look fuller in places where volume has thinned or never been prominent: under-eye hollows, smile lines, lips, upper eyelids, cheeks, and, in the maker's own marketing, breasts, buttocks and hands. On looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a topical alternative to injectable filler, with members posting before-and-after photographs.[3][4][5][6]

Sederma says sarsasapogenin promotes differentiation of pre-adipocytes (immature fat cells) into mature ones and encourages lipid storage, so that fat cells in the treated area enlarge. The company's data include cell-culture results and a 2006 in vivo study on breasts. Facial use has not been tested in a published trial, and published commentary on the ingredient describes its facial effects as anecdotal.[2][6]

paras: Volufiline is sold to cosmetic formulators as a pale, oil-based liquid that is mixed into the oil phase of creams, serums and emulsions. The manufacturer's data sheet lists it as preservative free, with a recommended use level of 5 percent in the finished product, and gives an example body-care emulsion at that concentration.[2] The ratio of carrier to extract is not publicly disclosed.[1][6]

Finished products range from single-ingredient oils and droppers sold online to serums and balms from mainstream skincare brands. A skincare review by Dr Rachel Ho lists a serum containing 92 percent Volufiline with a peptide, marketed for under-eyes, cheeks and smile lines, as well as a PDRN balm stick and a cream-in-serum from other brands.[6]

sections.h: Mechanism as described by the manufacturer
paras: Sederma's data sheet states that sarsasapogenin acts on a differentiation pathway involving PPAR gamma, COPS3 and COPS5; increases lipid incorporation through the glucose and fructose pathway (adipophilin, SLC2A5/GLUT5); and promotes anchoring of fatty tissue in the extracellular matrix (LOX, ECM2). It describes the result as a lipofilling-like effect, with enlarged adipocytes in the fatty tissue.[2] The company says these pathways were identified with DNA-array technique.[2]

The cell-culture results on the sheet used 3T3-L1 pre-adipocytes and adipocytes at a 1 percent concentration of the ingredient (equivalent to 10 micromolar sarsasapogenin). Sederma reports 201 percent more pre-adipocyte differentiation by a G3PDH activity marker, 32 percent more adipocyte proliferation, and a 641 percent rise in lipid storage by red-oil staining.[2]

Reviewers note that these are cell-culture findings and that the ingredient would have to pass through the skin to the subcutaneous fat layer of the face to act there. One skincare review by Dr Rachel Ho also observes that a product that truly changed fat-cell function would arguably be a drug rather than a cosmetic.[6]

Sederma has been part of Croda since 1997, and Volufiline was developed in the 2000s as a cosmetic alternative to surgical lipofilling, initially aimed at the bust and body.[1] The maker's data sheet bears a patent number (WO 2008/015639) and a claim-substantiation page dated October 2006; the product reached the market in 2008, according to one encyclopedia summary.[1][2]

Its move into face and beauty culture came later. Social media posts, in particular on TikTok, described it as filler in a bottle, and mainstream beauty outlets ran explainers on whether it works.[7][6] The Ordinary and other brands launched facial products built around the ingredient.[6] On looksmax.org, threads on using it for under-eye hollows, upper-eyelid fat, lips and smile lines run over several years and include an update thread, a comparison with hyaluronic acid for dark circles, and requests for where to buy.[3][4][5]

In a widely read looksmax.org thread, a member shows photographs of a thin upper lip and a deep labiomental crease before use and after two to three months, and says it worked but took a while. His routine: a drop of the product on the area each night, left on overnight, sometimes mixed with a moisturizer or beef tallow to help it stay put.[3] Other threads discuss use on under-eyes, the upper eyelid, and as a replacement for filler.[4][5]

Members also dispute it. One thread argues that Sederma no longer exists as a separate company because Croda bought it, that bottles sold as pure Volufiline under the Sederma name make little sense, that the main paper dates from 2006, and that there is little independent reporting on it.[7] Replies in that thread include members who say they saw no results.[7]

Manufacturers and reviewers list mild irritation, redness, itching and allergic reactions as the main reported effects, particularly in sensitive skin.[1] A skincare review by Dr Rachel Ho raises the question of unwanted fat growth in the face if the ingredient does act on fat cells, noting that no facial safety trials exist.[6] The volume effect is described as reversible once use stops.[1]
The ingredient is regulated as a cosmetic raw material rather than a drug in the EU and the United States.[1]

The main human data is Sederma's own in vivo breast study dated 2006. Reported summaries describe 28 women evaluable at day 56, a 5 percent preparation applied to one breast, and an average volume increase of 2.2 percent against 0.9 percent in controls (p=0.10), with best responders reaching 8.4 percent; the 8.4 percent figure appears on the manufacturer's sheet as the best-case improvement.[1][2][6] A skincare review by Dr Rachel Ho notes the study compared two breasts of the same person, did not account for hormonal fluctuation, was not published in a peer-reviewed journal and that the average gain may not be visible to the eye.[6]

No published trial has tested Volufiline on lips, under-eyes, cheeks or other facial areas. Separately, laboratory research on the plant compound has looked at fat tissue in other contexts: a 2021 study in obese mice fed a high-fat diet found that oral sarsasapogenin reduced adipose tissue inflammation and improved insulin resistance,[8] and a 2009 phytochemistry study examined constituents of Anemarrhena asphodeloides rhizomes that inhibit fat-cell formation.[9] These studies used oral dosing in animals or cell models and did not test topical cosmetic use.

lore.intro: Volufiline is a recurring topic in looksmax.org skincare threads, mainly for under-eyes, upper eyelids and lips, where members share photo updates and argue over whether the results are real and which products contain the genuine ingredient.[3][4][7][5]

claims.claim: Volufiline can rebuild lip and under-eye volume over a few months.
It works by making local fat cells grow and store more lipid.
The ingredient or the bottles sold under its name are not what they claim.
Volufiline is a safe, natural alternative to injectable filler.
Results fade once you stop using it.

timeline.event: Sederma becomes part of Croda International.[1]
Sederma's claim-substantiation data for Volufiline, including the 56-day breast study and 3T3-L1 cell-culture results, are dated October 2006.[2]
Volufiline reported to be launched commercially; the associated patent is WO 2008/015639.[1][2]
Phytochemistry study of Anemarrhena asphodeloides rhizome constituents that inhibit fat-cell formation published.[9]
Mouse study reports oral sarsasapogenin reducing adipose inflammation and insulin resistance on a high-fat diet.[8]
Volufiline serums from mainstream skincare brands and TikTok coverage bring the ingredient into beauty media; looksmax.org threads track personal results for lips and under-eyes.[3][7][6]
